review_notes: Duplicates row 17’s offense-stated consequence and adds only the direct disposition.
Correctly infers that induced securities purchases involved followers parting with money, a protected property interest.
Correctly applies Ciminelli to the district court’s information-only theory.
Correctly identifies the information-only alternative as the right-to-control theory rejected in Ciminelli.
Correctly applies Kousisis to explain why profit rather than intended net harm did not defeat intent to defraud.
Repeats the money-as-thing-of-value concept covered more centrally by row 1.
Duplicates row 10’s fraudulent-inducement injury concept, with a less precise target.
Correctly explains why mail-and-wire-fraud precedents informed the section 1348 analysis.
The target does not cleanly complete the cloze and leaves the counterfactual conclusion ambiguous.
Correctly applies the fraud-completion rule to the alleged induced purchase of securities.
The remaining-defendants point is procedural and mostly follows directly from Knight’s plea and the remand.
The material-element answer is a generic restatement of the sufficiency standard after listing the elements.
The two disputed elements are stated directly in one sentence.
The follower purchase step is a direct lookup from the pump-and-dump sequence.
Valid counterfactual applying the material-misrepresentation requirement to truthful posts.
The remand phrase is direct disposition language and does not add meaningful composition.
Correctly combines the review standard with the merits holding to conclude the indictment stated an offense.
